description.narrative: ltpgtProject targets critical protection challenges across four locations: Sweida (Malh and Mazraa), Quneitra, and Sheikh Miskin in Dar’a. These areas have been severely affected by years of conflict, insecurity, and climate change, which have disrupted agriculture, livestock, and livelihoods—the primary income sources for most families. The prolonged conflict and ongoing instability have led to widespread infrastructure damage, diminished access to essential services, and increased vulnerabilities, especially for displaced populations, PWDs, elderly, and female-headed households. In Sweida most households rely on agriculture and livestock However, conflict and environmental challenges have deepened socio-economic distress Quneitra face issues, with additional damage to infrastructure and reduced availability of services for PWDs and the elderly. In Sheikh Miskin, families contend with deteriorating public services, fewer livelihood opportunities, and higher protection concerns due to sustained socio-economic stressltbrgtFollowing the change in Dec 2024, returns to Dar’a and Quneitra have increased significantly. This influx, coinciding with major cuts in donor funding and the withdrawal of humanitarian actors, has resulted in the closure of nearly half of UNHCR-supported community centers Consequently, fragile infrastructure and services are further strained, exacerbating risks for returnees and host communityltbrgtProtection risks have intensified due to insecurity and worsening economic conditions. Families suffer from increased psychosocial distress, leading to harmful coping mechanisms such as child neglect, early marriage, and domestic and gender-based violence (GBV), including intimate partner violence, psychological abuse, and sexual exploitation, primarily affecting women and girls. Child protection concerns are rising, with elevated school dropouts, child labor, exposure to explosive ordnance, bullying, and interpersonal violence—symptoms of long-term psychological trauma aggravated by the absence of specialized mental health and referral servicesltbrgtThese overlapping vulnerabilities necessitate an integrated, multi-sectoral response addressing child protection, GBV, PSS, L.H, and education. BACC’s project design is based on comprehensive needs assessments, OCHA vulnerability criteria, and local response priorities, which justify the distribution of beneficiaries across the four sites to ensure tailored interventionsltbrgtThe integrated approach aims to reduce protection risks within each household by linking protection, and education components and facilitating referrals between programs for holistic support. Protection activities empowered marginalized groups—including female-headed households, returnees, families with PWDs or elderly members, and at-risk children—through community-based psychosocial support, awareness sessions, and strengthened community engagement and accountability mechanisms. The education component provides formal education, remedial learning for out-of-school children, safe inclusive environments, and distribution of school kits as neededltbrgtAll activities adhere to humanitarian principles of neutrality, impartiality, and inclusivity, applying a community-based approach sensitive to AGD and ensuring full compliance with Protection from PSEA standardsltbrgtThis multi-sectoral integration not only addresses immediate needs but also enhances community resilience and sustainable recovery, with continuous monitoring and evaluation to adapt interventions responsively.BACC ensures that no vulnerable group is left behind, particularly PWDsltbrgtAreas facing insecurity, weak infrastructure, economic decline affecting households. School dropout rates reach 21% Sweida, 17% Quneitra, 24% Dara’a Issues like child labor (up to 23%), domestic violence up to 33% and psychological distress up to 25% lt/pgt
